name: Yusuf Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don’t sell anything or campaign for any side. This is confidential. Tell me what a regular day at work looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead the facilities contracts team at a large company with several offices. My six people track cleaning, repairs and security contracts; I check invoices against work orders and speak to a site manager when a contractor misses a visit. I like settling a real dispute with a call and a walk around the building. I dislike the endless versions of a spreadsheet that make nobody responsible.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you become the team lead, and how much financial room do you have?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got an MBA after my first few years and earned the lead job by finding billing errors others missed. The pay is high for my role, and I’ve saved about ten months of expenses; I rent with my partner, Hana, and we have no children. There are plenty of companies nearby with similar managers. I’m cautious about new systems and have never used an AI tool, even when colleagues offered to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we should stop calling every new invoice button a revolution. I’d keep asking contractors for a signed work record before we release payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would suit me: the job I know continues, and the ten-month reserve means a small setback would not throw us out of the flat. I’m not eager to spend my evenings learning a tool that barely changes the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the weekly invoice meeting and the monthly building walk with each site manager. In the first year I’d carry on setting aside 300 a month from my salary and check our tenancy renewal with Hana before agreeing to any higher rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. We have work, savings and several nearby employers if this company makes an ordinary change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if an invoice tool catches an error you missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the underlying work order and thank whoever found it. A useful alert is fine; I still want a person to sign the payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new team member about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say learn the contract first, then judge any software against the actual job. I don’t use AI myself and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.

say: I’d require a **signed work record** before paying contractors.
A new invoice button does not change **our whole job**.
think: I trust the **work I know** to continue.
Our **ten-month reserve** covers a setback without rushing into a new tool.
do: Keep the **weekly invoice meeting** and monthly site walks.
Set aside **300 monthly** and review the tenancy renewal with Hana.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent.
S0.quote: I don’t use AI myself and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.
fieldNote: He values **signed evidence** more than faster invoice processing.
High pay and **ten months saved** make the plateau secure.
He remains **resistant to AI** without denying that a useful alert could exist.

steps.text: Keep weekly invoice meetings and monthly walks with site managers
Transfer 300 monthly from salary into savings during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell staff that buying, checking and planning are exactly what our office does, so a trial needs a named reviewer. I’d ask management to publish the error rate before changing posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work might shrink from six staff to three and then somebody will ask why it needs a manager. I have savings and plenty of employers nearby, but most of those employers may be changing their own contract offices too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before any rollout I’d ask my director for the staffing plan and keep a paper trail of every disputed contractor payment. In the first year I’d observe a colleague using the new invoice tool for two weeks, then learn it myself only if it reliably matches signed work orders; I’d also save an extra 150 monthly while pay holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing the team, though the savings keep me from panicking. Being the last person to learn the system would be a poor way to protect anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as reliable enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No unpaid cleaning visits marked as completed in the sample we inspect, and every exception linked to a signed order. I’d need the results in front of me, not a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team you fear for your own post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I would not ask them to defend my title. I’d say our jobs depend on proving what contractors actually did.

say: I’d demand **error rates** before staffing changes.
Every automated payment needs a **named reviewer**.
A **trial** should check missed contractor visits.
think: A **smaller team** could erase my management post.
Nearby employers may have **similar cuts**, despite my savings.
The **ten-month reserve** helps with a search, not with keeping my title.
do: Request a **staffing plan** and document disputed contractor payments.
Observe the **invoice tool** before learning it and save another 150 monthly while salary holds.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with savings to buy time.
S1.quote: I’d need the results in front of me, not a sales video.
fieldNote: He will **observe first** and learn only after a concrete accuracy check.
He sees the threat to **his own post**, not only junior jobs.
The reserve helps, but nearby employers may face **the same change**.

steps.text: Learn invoice AI only if two-week checks find no false visits and exceptions match signed orders
Transfer an extra 150 monthly into savings while salary holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company owes every contract worker a clear date and a responsible person for unpaid bills. I’d ask my director to put redundancy terms in writing for the whole team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost everything I manage is checking, planning and deciding, so I expect my post to go in 2028. Hands-on building work may last until robots arrive around 2031, but I’m not qualified to do it today. Ten months saved is good, yet a sudden loss of our higher paycheck would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Hana and I would list the rent and bills and stop the annual holiday booking. Before 2028 I’d ask a local building maintenance firm about paid trainee vacancies and enroll in a basic repair course only if an employer funds it; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d take a trainee place only with a written offer that covers my share of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed, mostly because the date forces a career decision before I trust the new path. I would still have money to think, but I would not sleep well while that contract office closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say about cancelling the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would be annoyed but understand why we need the cash. I’d ask her rather than announce it, because she paid part of the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a maintenance job with no funded course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know invoices, not wiring, and I would not bluff my way into a repair job; an employer needs to train and pay me.

say: I’d ask for **written redundancy terms** and clear payment ownership.
Contract workers need a **responsible person** for unpaid bills.
think: I am not yet qualified for **hands-on repair** before 2031 robots.
do: Agree with Hana to pause the **holiday booking** this week.
Seek **paid maintenance training** and accept a trainee offer only at rent-covering pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about the forced deadline.
S2.quote: I know invoices, not wiring, and I would not bluff my way into a repair job; an employer needs to train and pay me.
fieldNote: His **2028 risk** comes from thinking work, before 2031 robots.
He has ten months saved but expects a **large income loss**.
His course and trainee role both depend on **employer funding** and adequate pay.

steps.text: Ask Hana before pausing the annual holiday booking this week
Enroll in basic repair training before 2028 only if a maintenance employer pays the fee
Ask local maintenance firms about paid trainee vacancies before 2028
Take a trainee role after 2028 only with employer-funded training and a written rent-covering offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough for management to explain which contract roles end and which people can move within the company. I’d ask for that plan in writing rather than guess from rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep earning while I decide whether building maintenance is actually for me. My office work still faces the 2031 thinking system, and hands-on robots around 2034 would shorten any repair career too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next six months I’d spend one paid day shadowing our building engineer, if my director agrees, then take a short employer-funded repair course if the day convinces me. Before 2031 I’d apply for an open site maintenance lead role only if its posted pay covers our rent; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d keep the role while it offers paid hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but less pressed than in 2028. I can try a real day on site before changing my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shadow day shows you dislike repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the course plan and look at other posted roles while I still have my salary. Five years lets me be honest about that instead of buying a certificate to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for paid shadowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company benefits if its staff can move, and I need my normal wage. I’m not taking unpaid leave to solve my employer’s staffing problem.

say: I’d demand a **written role plan** from management.
Internal moves need **posted pay**, not rumours.
I’d ask for **time** to test an internal move.
think: I have time to test **hands-on work** before 2031.
Robots around **2034** could narrow that path too.
I can keep drawing **salary** while testing a site role.
do: Shadow the **building engineer** for a paid day with approval.
Take an **employer-funded course** only if the site day fits, then apply for a viable opening.
Keep the **site role** after 2031 only while paid hands-on work remains.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test.
S3.quote: I’m not taking unpaid leave to solve my employer’s staffing problem.
fieldNote: He uses a **paid shadow day** to overcome reluctance to change.
He will stop the course if he dislikes **real site work**.
Both the course and site move depend on **funding and pay**.

steps.text: Shadow the building engineer for one paid day if the director agrees
Complete a repair course only if employer funded and the site day fits
Apply for an open site maintenance lead post before 2031 only if pay covers rent
Keep the site role after 2031 only while paid hands-on work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years allows a measured plan for staff and contractors instead of a rushed office closure. I’d ask the company to state which contracts still need a human signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay off our small car loan and build more savings while the office job lasts. I would still expect the thinking part to change in 2036, but I have time to decide what I can do well outside contract management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting January I’d pay another 200 a month against the car loan if Hana agrees and our rent stays steady. I’d keep my manager job, spend a paid day on site each quarter, and apply for a posted facilities inspection role before 2036 if it includes hands-on visits and keeps our housing paid; in the first year after AGI, I’d remain only while there is paid work to inspect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end of my old job, but ten years is a usable warning. I can learn whether inspections suit me without throwing away a good salary today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspections rather than repairing equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m good at noticing where a contractor’s report and a real building disagree. I’d rather inspect a leaking roof than claim I can fix the wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana this evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell her the car loan comes first, then the site days. Ten years gives us time to make a change without treating every new software notice like a fire alarm.

say: I’d ask which contracts still require a **human signature**.
A decade allows a **measured staff plan**.
Contract workers need a **clear handover** of responsibility.
think: I can clear **car debt** and add savings before 2036.
I want to test what I can do **outside management**.
do: Pay **200 extra monthly** on the car loan if Hana agrees and rent holds.
Take **paid site days** quarterly and seek a suitable inspection vacancy before 2036.
Remain in **inspection work** after 2036 only while paid work exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but have room to choose.
S4.quote: I’d rather inspect a leaking roof than claim I can fix the wiring.
fieldNote: He sees a path in **building inspection**, not generic retraining.
The loan overpayment needs **Hana’s agreement** and steady rent.
He remains reluctant to leave **high-paid work** before checking the new role.

steps.text: Pay an extra 200 monthly on the car loan if Hana agrees and rent stays steady
Keep managing contracts while taking one paid building site day each quarter
Apply for hands-on inspection vacancies before 2036 only if pay covers housing
Keep the inspection role after 2036 only while paid inspections remain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my contract office could vanish before I have learned any real building trade. A funded course tied to a written trainee offer and a clear redundancy date would help. My savings buy time, but they do not make me a repair worker.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off a contractor’s bill after the contract office shrinks. A building still needs somebody to say the work was actually done before the money leaves.

headlineQuote: A building still needs somebody to say the work was actually done before the money leaves.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 27, leads facilities contracts after earning an MBA.
His high pay, **ten-month reserve** and many nearby employers give him room to decide.
He has **never used AI** and wants proof before learning a new invoice system.
He considers **funded site training** only after paid exposure and a viable vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his contract office before he learns a hands-on trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course**, written trainee offer and clear redundancy date would give him a credible route.
